title: Epilepsy Medication Manufacturing
one_liner: US epilepsy medication manufacturing is a specialized pharma niche where steady patient need supports demand, while patent cliffs, generic entry and rare-epilepsy launches reshape revenue mix.
overview: This industry covers companies that research, develop, manufacture and commercialize anti-seizure medications for epilepsy, including branded drugs, orphan-drug therapies and generics. The 2022 IBIS baseline estimated US epilepsy medication manufacturing revenue at $6.553 billion, but public 2025 market trackers define the addressable US epilepsy treatment-drug market more narrowly, with 2025 values around $3.2 billion and 2024 values between $3.1 billion and $3.9 billion depending on methodology. Demand remains structurally resilient because epilepsy is chronic, medication is the first-line treatment, and CDC data for 2021-2022 reported about 2.9 million US adults plus about 456,000 US children with active epilepsy. Revenue quality is increasingly bifurcated: branded and orphan therapies retain premium pricing where patents and indications protect them, while mature molecules such as lacosamide, pregabalin, levetiracetam and perampanel face generic competition.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 US epilepsy treatment-drug market estimated at $3.2 billion by Global Market Insights; Grand View Research reported $3.8816 billion for the US epilepsy drugs market in 2024 and a 2025-2030 CAGR of 5.4%.
key_stats.growth: 2025-2034 US epilepsy treatment-drug CAGR estimated at 4.4%; 2025-2030 US epilepsy drugs CAGR estimated at 5.4%.
key_stats.patients: 2021-2022 CDC data reported about 2.9 million US adults with active epilepsy; 2022 child data reported about 456,000 US children with active epilepsy.
key_stats.health_spending: 2019 US health care spending for epilepsy and seizures alone was $24.5 billion, including $5.4 billion for epilepsy and $19.0 billion for seizures.
key_stats.branded_sales_examples: 2025 Epidiolex/Epidyolex net product sales were $1.059 billion at Jazz; 2025 UCB epilepsy-related product sales included Briviact at €758 million, Keppra at €439 million, Fintepla at €427 million, Vimpat at €303 million and Nayzilam at €128 million.

baseline_2022.market_size: $6.553 billion in 2022 IBIS industry revenue, stated in 2022 dollars.
baseline_2022.growth: 1.9% expected revenue growth in 2022; 2017-2022 revenue CAGR of 5.5%; 2022-2027 forecast CAGR of 3.8%.
baseline_2022.profit: $452 million in 2022 profit, equal to a 6.9% margin.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling branded and generic anti-seizure medicines to wholesalers, specialty distributors, hospital channels, retail pharmacies and government or commercial payers. Branded products make money through patent-protected pricing, orphan-drug exclusivity, specialty distribution and lifecycle management such as new indications, pediatric labeling, rescue formulations and extended-release dosing. Generic manufacturers compete on scale, ANDA approvals, supply reliability and pharmacy-benefit placement after patent expirations.
cost_structure: Major costs include active pharmaceutical ingredients and excipients, validated manufacturing capacity, quality systems, regulatory compliance, pharmacovigilance, clinical development, patent litigation, sales access teams, rebates and payer concessions. Generic producers carry lower R&D and marketing costs but heavier price competition; branded producers carry higher R&D, commercialization and postmarket study costs but can earn higher gross margins while exclusivity lasts. Baseline 2022 IBIS profit margin was 6.9%, while large branded pharma portfolios often report much higher product gross margins before R&D, SG&A and amortization.

{'name': 'Jazz Pharmaceuticals', 'position': 'Owner of Epidiolex/Epidyolex, which reported 2025 net product sales of $1.059 billion and 2026 Q1 revenue growth of 15% year over year.'}

{'name': 'SK Biopharmaceuticals / SK Life Science', 'position': 'Markets Xcopri/cenobamate for adult partial-onset seizures, a newer branded focal-seizure therapy.'}
{'name': 'Generic manufacturers', 'position': "Includes Teva, MSN Laboratories, Navinta, Dr. Reddy's, Lupin, Sun Pharma and other ANDA-focused firms competing after patent cliffs."}
current_dynamics: The industry is in a post-Vimpat, post-Lyrica patent-cliff environment where mature molecule revenue is shifting toward generics, but branded growth persists in rare and refractory epilepsy. Second-generation and third-generation anti-seizure drugs are gaining share because physicians value tolerability, fewer interactions and simpler dosing. Rescue therapies and pediatric formulations remain active niches, but regulatory and litigation outcomes can quickly alter launch timing. Payers continue to pressure branded pricing because generic prescriptions account for most volume, while branded drugs capture a disproportionate share of spending.
whats_growing: Rare epilepsy therapies with orphan or protected indications, including Epidiolex for LGS, Dravet syndrome and TSC and Fintepla for severe developmental epileptic encephalopathies.
Second-generation anti-seizure medications, which held a reported 47.3% share of the US epilepsy treatment-drug market in 2024 and are forecast to grow through 2034.
Oral and patient-friendly formulations, including extended-release products and rescue medicines designed for caregiver administration outside hospitals.
R&D for refractory epilepsy, pediatric epilepsy, genetic epilepsies and therapies with cleaner safety or drug-interaction profiles.
Specialty-support programs that help with diagnosis, prior authorization, adherence and rare-epilepsy patient services.
whats_shrinking: Revenue from older branded products after loss of exclusivity, including Vimpat/lacosamide after 2022 and Lyrica/pregabalin after 2019.
Price realization for molecules exposed to multiple ANDA entrants, including perampanel generics approved in 2025.
Brand share in high-volume seizure-control prescriptions where pharmacists and payers can substitute lower-cost generics.
Profit margins for smaller manufacturers without differentiated IP, specialty access or scale in generic supply.
Products dependent on narrow pediatric rescue indications when litigation or exclusivity disputes disrupt FDA approvals.
recent_developments: 2024-05-15: CDC reported about 2.9 million US adults with active epilepsy in 2021-2022 and about 456,000 US children with active epilepsy in 2022.
2025-05-23: FDA listed first generic approval for perampanel tablets, referencing Fycompa, for partial-onset seizures in patients with epilepsy aged 4 years and older.
2025-07-11: FDA listed first generic approval for perampanel oral suspension, referencing Fycompa suspension, for partial-onset seizures in patients with epilepsy aged 4 years and older.
2025-11-14: FDA listed first generic approval for diazepam rectal gel delivery system, referencing Diastat/Diastat AcuDial, for seizure clusters in patients with epilepsy aged 2 years and older.
2026-02-24: Jazz reported 2025 Epidiolex/Epidyolex net product sales of $1.059 billion, up 9% from 2024.
2026-02-26: UCB reported 2025 Briviact sales of €758 million and noted Briviact loss of exclusivity in the US and Europe in 2026.
outlook: Through 2026-2030, US epilepsy medication manufacturing should grow at a mid-single-digit rate in market-demand terms, but manufacturer revenue will depend heavily on portfolio mix. Growth will come from rare-epilepsy brands, newer focal-seizure drugs, pediatric indications, rescue formulations and better adherence tools. The main headwinds are patent cliffs, ANDA launches, rebate pressure, payer step edits and the high cost of clinical trials in small epilepsy subpopulations. Companies with protected brands and credible pipelines should outperform, while single-product or mature-brand portfolios will be exposed to rapid generic erosion.

title: Family Counseling & Crisis Intervention Services in the US
one_liner: A fragmented, mostly nonprofit social-assistance industry funded by government grants, donations and sliding-scale client fees, with demand lifted by mental health, substance use, homelessness and crisis-line needs.
overview: The industry sits at the intersection of behavioral health and social assistance. Operators include local nonprofits, community agencies, crisis centers, faith-based providers, family service organizations, recovery-support groups and some for-profit counseling platforms. IBISWorld's 2022 baseline placed 2021 industry revenue at $48.0 billion and projected real revenue of $52.4 billion by 2026. Current public indicators point to continued demand: SAMHSA's 2024 NSDUH reported 61.5 million adults with any mental illness and 48.4 million people aged 12 or older with a substance use disorder, while GAO reported 19.1 million routed 988 contacts from July 2022 through September 2025. Revenue remains highly dependent on federal, state and local funding cycles, Medicaid reimbursement, philanthropic giving and clients' ability to pay sliding-scale fees.

key_stats.market_size: 2026: $52.4 billion estimated industry revenue in 2021 dollars from the 2022 IBISWorld forecast; broader Census NAICS 6241 Individual and Family Services revenue reached $194.2 billion in 2025 and $49.3 billion in Q1 2026 seasonally adjusted.
key_stats.growth: 2021-2026: 1.8% forecast CAGR for the IBIS industry; broader Census NAICS 6241 revenue grew 7.5% in 2025 versus 2024 and Q1 2026 seasonally adjusted revenue was 6.5% above Q1 2025.
key_stats.employment: 2021: 501,550 industry workers in the IBIS baseline; broader BLS NAICS 6241 employment reached 3.7 million jobs in 2025.
key_stats.establishments: 2021: 103,643 industry establishments in the IBIS baseline; 2026 forecast was 114,106 establishments.
key_stats.profit_margin: 2021: 3.5% EBIT margin in the IBIS baseline, reflecting nonprofit reinvestment and labor intensity.
key_stats.demand_indicators: 2024: 61.5 million adults had any mental illness, 48.4 million people aged 12+ had a substance use disorder, and 48,824 suicide deaths were recorded in the US.

baseline_2022.growth: 2016-2021: 4.8% annualized revenue growth; 2021-2026 forecast: 1.8% annualized growth to $52.4 billion.
baseline_2022.profit: 2021: $1.7 billion EBIT, equal to a 3.5% margin.
baseline_2022.wages: 2021: $17.4 billion total wages, equal to about 36.3% of revenue.
baseline_2022.service_mix: 2021: social assistance services 40.2%, counseling services 36.5%, crisis intervention 9.6%, self-help groups 5.5%, shelter and food services 5.0%, immigrant and refugee assistance 2.2%, rehabilitative services 1.0%.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn revenue from federal, state and local grants; Medicaid and other public reimbursement; contracts with schools, courts, hospitals and public agencies; foundation grants; charitable donations; United Way and faith-based giving; and client fees charged on a sliding scale. Crisis centers and family-service nonprofits often blend restricted grants with unrestricted donations, while counseling providers may add fee-for-service sessions, employee-assistance referrals and telehealth reimbursement.

cost_structure.labor: 2021: wages were about 36.3% of revenue in the IBIS baseline; 2024 BLS reported $59,190 median pay for substance abuse, behavioral disorder and mental health counselors, and projected 17% occupational employment growth from 2024 to 2034.
cost_structure.profit: 2021: EBIT margin was 3.5%, low because many operators are nonprofits that reinvest surpluses and rely on grant compliance spending.
cost_structure.program_costs: 2025-2026: grant-funded programs require spending on counselors, supervisors, case managers, peer specialists, hotline infrastructure, data reporting, outreach, facilities, transportation, insurance and compliance.
cost_structure.funding_risk: 2026: first-round SAMHSA block-grant allocations totaled $794 million, but timing, renewals and federal program priorities remain a key budget risk for providers.

major_players: Vibrant Emotional Health / 988 Lifeline administrator network
United Way Worldwide and local United Way agencies
Catholic Charities USA member agencies
Volunteers of America affiliates
The Salvation Army social services
Boys Town family and crisis services
The Trevor Project and other specialized crisis-service nonprofits
Local community mental health centers, CCBHCs and family service agencies
current_dynamics: Demand is structurally elevated but uneven by service line. 988 has expanded the visible crisis-intervention market, with GAO reporting call volume up 87%, text volume up 260% and chat volume up 23% from July 2022 to September 2025. CCBHCs are shifting some providers toward Medicaid-backed, comprehensive behavioral-health models with 24/7 crisis requirements. Funding remains supportive in parts of the market: SAMHSA announced 2026 block-grant allocations, 988 capacity grants and CCBHC funding opportunities. At the same time, providers face counselor shortages, higher wage expectations, documentation burden, technology costs and policy uncertainty around specialized programs and federal reorganization priorities.
whats_growing: 988 call, text and chat crisis capacity, including local routing, follow-up programs and state/territory cooperative agreements.
CCBHC-linked crisis, case-management, peer-support and outpatient behavioral-health services backed by Medicaid demonstration or state-plan reimbursement.
Substance-use treatment navigation, recovery support and family counseling tied to opioid, alcohol and polysubstance needs.
Telehealth, hybrid counseling, chat-based crisis support and data/reporting systems required by grants and payers.
School, youth, trauma-informed and family-support services as adolescent anxiety, depression and suicide-risk needs remain visible in 2024 data.
whats_shrinking: COVID-era emergency funding is no longer the same growth engine that boosted 2020-2021 revenue.
Standalone preventive or low-acuity programs are more vulnerable when grants are redirected to crisis, overdose, homelessness or serious-mental-illness priorities.
Small nonprofits without Medicaid billing, grant-writing scale or workforce depth face margin pressure and potential consolidation.
Specialized federally funded 988 subnetworks became more exposed to appropriations timing, highlighted by the July 2025 discontinuation of the LGBTQ+ youth Press 3 option.
Client self-pay capacity remains constrained for low-income households, limiting fee growth despite strong need.
recent_developments: 2025-07-17: SAMHSA discontinued the 988 LGBTQ+ youth and young adult Press 3 subnetwork after allocated funding was expended.
2025-07-28: SAMHSA released 2024 NSDUH results showing 61.5 million adults with any mental illness and 48.4 million people aged 12+ with a substance use disorder.
2026-02-04: SAMHSA distributed a first 2026 block-grant allocation of $794 million, including $319 million for MHBG and $475 million for SUBG.
2026-05-28: HHS selected 10 additional states for the CCBHC Medicaid Demonstration, with starts between July 1, 2026 and July 1, 2027.
2026-06-17: SAMHSA posted more than $700 million in behavioral-health funding opportunities, including $238.6 million for 988 and suicide crisis Lifeline programs and $223.1 million for CCBHCs.
2026-07-01: GAO reported 19.1 million routed 988 contacts from July 2022 through September 2025, with September 2025 call volume at 460,264.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but funding-sensitive. Demand should remain high because mental illness, substance-use disorders, suicide risk, homelessness and family stress continue to generate referrals. The strongest operators will be those that can combine grant funding with Medicaid reimbursement, 988/CCBHC participation, measurable outcomes and workforce retention. Revenue growth is likely to be steadier than the 2020-2021 pandemic surge, with upside from crisis-system buildout and downside from federal budget shifts, expiring grants and labor scarcity.

title: Family Planning & Abortion Clinics in the US
one_liner: A safety-net reproductive health industry growing modestly as contraception demand, public funding and telehealth offset post-Dobbs clinic disruption.
overview: This industry includes freestanding outpatient clinics providing contraception, genetic and prenatal counseling, voluntary sterilization, pregnancy testing, STI services and medication or procedural abortion. The 2022 IBIS baseline placed revenue at $3.7 billion, with a 2.0% 2017-2022 CAGR and a 1.8% 2022-2027 forecast CAGR. By 2025-2026, the market is still anchored by recurring preventive care and publicly funded safety-net services, but the operating map is more fragmented: 13 states had total abortion bans in 2025, 13 states still had total bans as of April 27, 2026, and patients increasingly travel or use telehealth where legal.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated revenue: about $3.9 billion, derived from the 2022 IBIS baseline of $3.73 billion and its 1.8% 2022-2027 forecast CAGR; latest public Census/FRED NAICS 621410 employer revenue totaled $3.891 billion in 2022 across taxable and tax-exempt firms.
key_stats.establishments: 2022 IBIS baseline: 2,607 establishments; 2023 Census Business Patterns for NAICS 621410 reported 3,591 employer establishments.
key_stats.employment: 2022 IBIS baseline: 27,750 workers; 2027 baseline forecast: 30,921 workers.
key_stats.title_x: FY2026 Title X Services awards listed by HHS TAGGS totaled $262.2 million; FY2027 services NOFO anticipated up to $257.0 million for up to 90 awards.
key_stats.abortion_volume: Guttmacher estimated 1,129,650 clinician-provided abortions in 2025, roughly flat versus 1,124,470 in 2024; Society of Family Planning estimated 1,126,760 abortions in the formal healthcare system in 2025.
key_stats.telehealth: Society of Family Planning reported more than 300,000 abortions via telehealth in 2025 and 29% of US abortions via telehealth by December 2025.

baseline_2022.service_mix: 2022 revenue mix: oral pill contraceptives 39.6%, long-acting contraceptives 25.3%, abortion services 15.3%, injectable contraceptives 14.3%, hormone treatment 5.5%.

how_it_makes_money.public_reimbursement: Medicaid, public insurance and Title X-supported care fund low-income and uninsured patient services; 2023 Title X providers said third-party payers such as Medicaid and other insurance accounted for 56% of grantee revenue.
how_it_makes_money.private_pay: Out-of-pocket payments covered an estimated 19.4% of 2022 industry revenue in the IBIS baseline.
how_it_makes_money.grants_and_donations: Private contributions, gifts and grants represented an estimated 28.7% of 2022 industry revenue in the IBIS baseline.
how_it_makes_money.service_lines: Clinics bill or receive program support for contraception, STI testing and treatment, cancer screenings, pregnancy tests, fertility and sterilization services, and abortion where legal.

cost_structure.labor: Labor is the largest cost: 2022 wages were $1.534 billion, equal to about 41.1% of 2022 revenue.
cost_structure.profit: 2022 EBIT margin was 7.8%, below many healthcare service categories because of safety-net pricing, grant restrictions and staffing pressure.
cost_structure.clinical_supplies: Major variable costs include contraceptives, pharmaceuticals including mifepristone and misoprostol where legal, medical supplies, lab work and diagnostic services.
cost_structure.occupancy_and_admin: Rent, insurance, compliance, security, billing, EHR systems and grant reporting are meaningful fixed costs; post-2022 legal compliance and patient navigation costs have risen in restricted and receiving states.
cost_structure.funding_risk: Medicaid and Title X payment interruptions can quickly pressure clinic margins because many patients are uninsured or publicly insured.

major_players: Planned Parenthood Federation of America and local affiliates
State and local health department family planning programs
Independent nonprofit reproductive health clinics
Federally Qualified Health Centers offering Title X-supported family planning
Maine Family Planning
Health Imperatives
current_dynamics: The industry is being reshaped by a split between higher national abortion volumes and reduced local access in ban states. In 2025, clinician-provided abortions remained above pre-Dobbs levels at about 1.13 million, supported by travel, medication abortion and telehealth. At the same time, KFF reported 13 total-ban states as of April 27, 2026, and Guttmacher found brick-and-mortar abortion clinics in non-ban states declined 2% from March 2024 to December 2025. Public funding remains critical: FY2026 Title X services awards totaled $262.2 million, but 2025-2026 federal Medicaid restrictions on certain reproductive health entities increased financial stress for Planned Parenthood, Maine Family Planning and Health Imperatives.
whats_growing: Medication abortion and telehealth abortion where permitted: 2025 telehealth abortions exceeded 300,000 and reached 29% of abortions by December 2025.
Patient travel and navigation services from ban states to access states: Guttmacher reported 13% of 2025 abortions in non-ban states were obtained by out-of-state patients, versus 9% in 2020.
Demand for contraception, STI testing and preventive reproductive health services through safety-net providers; Title X served nearly 2.8 million clients in 2023, up 7% from 2022.
State replacement funding and private philanthropy in abortion-access states after 2022.
whats_shrinking: Brick-and-mortar abortion provision in restrictive states and some non-ban markets, with Guttmacher reporting a 2% net decline in brick-and-mortar abortion clinics from March 2024 to December 2025.
Medicaid-funded access at affected Planned Parenthood and similar providers during the July 2025-July 2026 federal reimbursement block.
In-person abortion share, as telehealth and virtual-only medication abortion take more volume.
Clinic financial flexibility in low-income markets because many patients rely on public insurance, sliding-fee discounts or free care.
recent_developments: 2025-06-26: The Supreme Court decided Medina v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic, limiting Medicaid beneficiaries' private enforcement route to challenge state exclusion of Planned Parenthood as a provider.
2025-07-04: Section 71113 of the 2025 federal budget reconciliation law began a one-year block on federal Medicaid payments to certain reproductive health entities that provide abortion care.
2025-12: Society of Family Planning reported 1,126,760 US abortions in the formal healthcare system for calendar 2025, with more than 300,000 via telehealth.
2026-02: Guttmacher reported brick-and-mortar abortion clinics in states without total bans were down 2% from March 2024 to December 2025.
2026-04-27: KFF counted 13 states with abortion banned, 28 with gestational limits and 9 states plus DC with no gestational limit.
2026-06: HHS TAGGS listed FY2026 Title X Services awards totaling $262.2 million.
outlook: Revenue is likely to grow slowly through 2027, near the baseline 1.8% CAGR path, but the mix will keep shifting. Contraception and preventive services remain stable recurring demand, while abortion-related revenue migrates toward access states, virtual providers and clinics able to absorb travel patients. The biggest downside risks are federal Medicaid restrictions, Title X policy changes, provider shortages, security and compliance costs, and state-level abortion bans. Upside comes from telehealth scale, pharmacy dispensing of mifepristone under FDA REMS rules, state access funds, private donations and continued demand from low-income patients who rely on safety-net clinics.
themes: Patient travel and state shield laws
Title X and Medicaid policy risk

title: Fantasy Sports Services
one_liner: Fantasy sports services monetize sports fandom through season-long leagues, daily contests, subscriptions, data tools, sponsorships and advertising.
overview: Fantasy sports services provide online and app-based games where users draft or select real athletes and score points from real-world sports performance. The industry includes season-long league platforms, daily fantasy sports contests, commissioner tools, player-news and analytics subscriptions, pick-based games, and related advertising or sponsorship inventory. The 2022 IBIS baseline described a growth industry recovering from 2020 sports cancellations, with revenue driven by advertising, mobile access and DFS adoption. By 2025-2026, the market is larger but more bifurcated: classic season-long fantasy and salary-cap DFS remain broadly available, while pick'em and against-the-house formats face tighter scrutiny in several states.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 U.S. fantasy sports revenue was $9.267 billion; 2026 estimated revenue was $10.264 billion.
key_stats.growth: 2026 estimated revenue implies 10.8% growth from 2025; Grand View Research projects an 11.2% CAGR for 2026-2033.
key_stats.participants: 2025 FSGA-published research cited 84 million U.S. and Canadian adults participating in fantasy sports or sports betting in the prior 12 months, including 77 million Americans; FSGA demographics cited 62.5 million U.S. and Canadian fantasy sports players in 2022.
key_stats.legal_footprint: As of March 2026, classic DFS was listed as legal in 41 states plus DC, while five states effectively banned DFS and pick'em products had a narrower legal footprint.
key_stats.baseline_segments: In the 2021 IBIS baseline, season-long fantasy services represented 45.3% of revenue, daily fantasy sports 40.3%, and other services 14.4%.
key_stats.profitability: The 2021 IBIS baseline estimated industry profit margin at 2.9% and projected 2026 profit margin at 2.8% because of competition and legal costs.

baseline_2022.market_size: 2022 estimated market size was about $9.06 billion, inferred from IBIS's 2021 revenue of $8.884 billion and 2021-2027 projected CAGR of 2.01%.
baseline_2022.growth: 2022 estimated growth was about 2.0%, consistent with the IBIS 2021-2027 projected CAGR.
baseline_2022.context: The 2022 baseline framed the industry as recovering from 2020 sports cancellations, with mobile access, online advertising, DFS adoption and female participation as growth drivers.

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn revenue from advertising and sponsorships on free fantasy products, subscriptions for premium tools and commissioner services, DFS contest entry fees or platform rake, paid league management features, affiliate and media partnerships, data products, branded games, and ancillary commerce such as events or merchandise. In 2025 public filings, DraftKings classified DFS within an 'Other' revenue category alongside digital lottery courier and prediction markets, while fantasy-first firms such as PrizePicks monetized DFS-style paid contests and free-to-play engagement products.
cost_structure: Major costs include prize payouts and contest operations, payment processing, cloud hosting, sports data feeds, engineering and product staff, customer support, cybersecurity and fraud controls, advertising and promotional credits, league or media partnerships, regulatory licensing, legal defense and compliance. The 2025 DraftKings filing illustrates the broader cost base for fantasy-adjacent operators: 2025 revenue of $6.055 billion was paired with 2025 cost of revenue of $3.557 billion, 2025 sales and marketing of $1.380 billion, 2025 product and technology expense of $460 million, and 2025 G&A of $674 million.
major_players: DraftKings: fantasy-rooted public operator with 2025 total revenue of $6.055 billion and 2025 U.S. revenue of $5.895 billion; 2025 'Other' revenue, including DFS, was $423 million.

FanDuel / Flutter Entertainment: major DFS and sportsbook brand; Flutter's U.S. segment generated 2025 revenue of $6.967 billion, with 2025 U.S. 'Other' revenue of $239 million and disclosed DFS migration toward sportsbook products.

PrizePicks: fantasy-first DFS operator; Allwyn agreed on September 22, 2025 to buy 62.3% of PrizePicks at a $2.5 billion upfront enterprise value, with potential value up to $4.15 billion over the next three years.
Underdog Fantasy: private fantasy-first challenger focused on pick'em, drafts and season-long products; 2026 availability varies by state as pick'em rules tighten.

Yahoo Fantasy, ESPN Fantasy and CBS Sports: large media-backed season-long fantasy platforms that monetize audience engagement through advertising, subscriptions, content, data and cross-promotion rather than only paid DFS rake.
FantasyPros and RotoWire: specialist data, advice and subscription platforms serving 2025-2026 fantasy players with projections, rankings and lineup tools.
current_dynamics: The market is growing in dollars but splitting by format. Season-long fantasy remains mainstream and sticky around NFL, NBA, MLB and college sports calendars. DFS contests still monetize high-intent users, but classic peer-to-peer formats face less regulatory friction than pick'em or against-the-house games. Operators are adding personalization, AI-assisted projections, faster contest loops and social features while managing higher marketing costs, product compliance costs and state-by-state product restrictions. Sports betting and prediction markets both compete with and feed fantasy engagement, creating cross-sell opportunities for diversified operators but also pulling some DFS users into licensed wagering products.
whats_growing: Growing areas include mobile-first gameplay, next-generation season-long formats, dynasty and keeper leagues, soccer, esports and non-NFL sports, subscription analytics, lineup optimizers, paid entry leagues, peer-to-peer tournament structures, free-to-play acquisition funnels, personalization, responsible-play tooling, and fantasy products tied to live media and streaming. The 2025 FSGA agenda emphasized next-generation season-long fantasy behavior, and 2026 market forecasts show 2026-2033 revenue CAGR of 11.2%.
whats_shrinking: Shrinking or pressured areas include desktop-first league management, undifferentiated free fantasy sites reliant only on display ads, older paid subscription products without mobile utility, DFS formats that resemble unlicensed sports betting, operator availability in states restricting pick'em contests, and fantasy-only revenue at diversified sportsbook operators where users migrate to sportsbook or iGaming products. Flutter disclosed that 2025 U.S. 'Other' revenue fell 8% because part of its DFS player base migrated to sportsbook play.
recent_developments: July 1, 2025: FSGA presented research on next-generation fantasy players, year-over-year U.S. and Canada participation, demographics, season-long formats and likelihood to expand into DFS and sports betting.

July 3, 2025: California DOJ released a formal legal opinion on daily fantasy sports, increasing uncertainty in the largest U.S. state even though the department said only lawmakers or voters can change state law.
September 22, 2025: Allwyn agreed to acquire 62.3% of PrizePicks for $1.6 billion cash, implying a $2.5 billion upfront enterprise value and up to $4.15 billion if three-year metrics are met.
December 31, 2025: DraftKings reported 2025 total revenue of $6.055 billion, with 2025 'Other' revenue of $423 million that primarily included DFS, digital lottery courier and prediction markets.
March 1, 2026: Odds Reference listed classic DFS as legal in 41 states plus DC and identified five states where DFS is effectively banned.
June 25, 2026: Grand View Research updated its U.S. fantasy sports outlook, estimating 2025 revenue at $9.267 billion, 2026 revenue at $10.264 billion and 2026-2033 CAGR at 11.2%.
outlook: The 2026 outlook is positive but more regulated and more competitive than the 2022 baseline implied. Revenue should keep rising as fantasy remains embedded in sports media, mobile usage, live stats, social play and paid contest behavior. The strongest operators will combine large user pools, trusted scoring, recognizable brands, flexible state-specific products, high-quality projections, lower acquisition costs and responsible-play compliance. The main risks are adverse state rulings, pick'em reclassification as sports betting, promotion-heavy competition, user migration to sportsbook or prediction-market products, and dependence on the sports calendar. A reasonable 2026 brief should treat the industry as a growth market with 2025 revenue around $9.27 billion and a 2026 estimate around $10.26 billion, rather than only the older IBIS 2026 forecast of $9.8 billion.

one_sentence: The U.S. fantasy sports services market remains a mobile-first digital entertainment category, with 2025 revenue near $9.27 billion and growth tied to sports media engagement, paid contest formats, data-driven tools and a volatile state regulatory map for daily fantasy and pick'em games.

title: Fine Arts Schools in the US
one_liner: A fragmented, tuition-led market for recreational dance, music, theater and visual arts instruction is rebuilding around in-person classes while using hybrid formats and donations to cushion discretionary demand swings.
overview: This industry covers non-degree instruction in dance, drama, music and visual arts, excluding academic fine arts degrees, commercial art and technical photography programs. The 2022 baseline was still recovering from the 2020 in-person services shock, but public 2024 IBISWorld market-size data show revenue had moved above the 2022 level even as 2024 growth turned slightly negative. Demand remains highly discretionary: parents pay for children's lessons, adults buy hobby and social classes, and pre-professional students pay for portfolio, audition and summer training. The market is locally fragmented, wage-intensive and location-dependent, with online instruction expanding the addressable market but also increasing price competition.

key_stats.arts_culture_humanities_giving: 2025: $27.31 billion, up 7.5% current dollars and 4.7% inflation-adjusted
key_stats.consumer_spending: June 2026: U.S. PCE +0.3% month over month; May 2026: +0.9%
key_stats.lesson_price_inflation: February 2026: fees for lessons or instructions +3.1% year over year

baseline_2022.revenue_mix: 2022: recreational dance classes 48.8%, recreational music and theater classes 16.3%, training and professional development 10.8%, contributions 9.1%, academic programs 6.1%, other 5.2%, recreational visual arts 3.7%

how_it_makes_money: Operators earn most revenue from tuition and class fees for recurring group classes, private lessons, workshops, camps, recitals, audition preparation and short professional-development courses. Secondary revenue comes from registration fees, performance fees, merchandise or materials, studio rentals, grants and charitable contributions, with 2022 contributions representing 9.1% of industry revenue in the baseline.
cost_structure: Costs are dominated by instructor and administrative wages, with 2022 wages of $2.125 billion equal to roughly 35.3% of 2022 revenue. Rent or mortgage costs for studios, utilities, insurance, marketing, payment processing, instruments, costumes, sets, art supplies and digital teaching platforms follow. Margins are thin because small class sizes, skilled teachers and leased studio space limit scale; 2022 EBIT profit margin was 5.8%.
major_players: No dominant national player; the 2022 baseline characterized concentration as low and the industry as locally fragmented.
Local dance studios, music schools, theater schools, visual arts studios and community arts nonprofits make up most operators.
Larger nonprofit arts centers, youth conservatories and multi-location lesson providers compete regionally, but market share is dispersed.
current_dynamics: 2025-2026 conditions are mixed. Household services spending is still growing, with BEA reporting 2026 monthly PCE gains, but families remain price-sensitive after several years of inflation and lesson fees were still up 3.1% year over year in February 2026. Public arts funding is steadier than the 2022 baseline expected, with NEA appropriations listed at $207.0 million in 2024, 2025 and 2026. Private giving is more supportive: Giving USA reported 2025 arts, culture and humanities giving at $27.31 billion, up 7.5% in current dollars. The operating challenge is converting that broader support into enrollment while absorbing wage, rent and insurance costs.
whats_growing: Hybrid lesson models, summer and school-break camps, adult hobby classes, pre-college audition and portfolio preparation, community partnerships with schools and museums, and short-format workshops are gaining because they widen schedules and allow operators to sell higher-value services. Philanthropic support improved in 2025, and stable 2026 NEA appropriations help nonprofits plan even if federal grant priorities shift.
whats_shrinking: Purely discretionary low-frequency classes, underfilled group lessons, operators dependent on weak local foot traffic, and programs with high facility needs but limited pricing power are under pressure. The 2024 market-size decline of -0.7% indicates the post-pandemic rebound cooled, and online alternatives continue to compress pricing for basic music, drawing and photography instruction.
recent_developments: 2024: IBISWorld public market-size data put Fine Arts Schools in the US at $7.3 billion, down 0.7% for the year.
2024: IBISWorld public data showed 2019-2024 market-size CAGR of 0.6%, signaling a slow recovery cycle after 2020 volatility.
2025: Giving USA reported arts, culture and humanities giving of $27.31 billion, up 7.5% in current dollars.
2025: NEA appropriation history listed 2025 funding at $207.0 million, flat with 2024.
2026: NEA appropriation history listed 2026 funding at $207.0 million, again flat year over year.
2026: BLS CPI data for February 2026 showed fees for lessons or instructions up 3.1% year over year.
outlook: The outlook is for low to modest growth rather than a breakout. The 2022 baseline forecast called for 2022-2027 revenue CAGR of 1.1% to $6.3 billion, while the later public IBISWorld 2024 market-size page already showed a larger 2024 base of $7.3 billion but a -0.7% annual decline. Through 2026, demand should benefit from services spending growth, steady public arts appropriations and stronger arts philanthropy, but operators will need disciplined scheduling, higher-value programs and teacher retention to protect margins as lesson-price inflation and household budget scrutiny continue.

one_sentence: Fine arts schools sell non-degree arts instruction to households, children, adult hobbyists and aspiring performers, with 2024 market size at $7.3 billion after -0.7% growth and 2025-2026 demand shaped by household spending, lesson-price inflation, arts giving and public funding stability.
